title: Which date suits you?
goal: Agree a day, a date and a time with Maryam, your colleague, for a work meeting.
tip: To fix a meeting, give the day or the date, then is-sāʿa and the hour, with no word for 'on' or 'at': yōm il-arbaʿa is-sāʿa tisiʿ (on Wednesday at nine). A date is the plain number: siṭṭaʿash (the 16th), thamanṭaʿash iṣ-ṣubḥ (the 18th, in the morning).
grammar: Day, date and time together: yōm il-arbaʿa, sabaʿṭaʿash, is-sāʿa tisiʿ
dialogue: سالم، نتلاقى في المكتب يوم الثلاثاء، سطعش؟
Sālim, nitlāga fi l-maktab yōm ith-thalātha, siṭṭaʿash?
Salim, shall we meet in the office on Tuesday, the sixteenth?
سطعش عندي موعد. يوم الأربعاء، سبعطعش؟
siṭṭaʿash ʿindi mawʿid. yōm il-arbaʿa, sabaʿṭaʿash?
On the sixteenth I've got an appointment. Wednesday, the seventeenth?
The seventeenth I can't. Does the eighteenth suit you?
Yes, it suits me. What time?
badri, is-sāʿa tisiʿ w rubʿ iṣ-ṣubḥ
Early: quarter past nine in the morning.
items: a date is the plain number: yōm siṭṭaʿash = on the 16th
does it suit you? (to a man)
to a woman: ynāsbich? (يناسبج); it suits me: ynāsibni; ma ynāsibni = it doesn't suit me

title: Come on, quick!
goal: A friend hurries you out of the door: get up, look, listen, take it, come.
tip: To tell a man to do something, drop the t- of the 'you' verb: tshūf → shūf (look), trūḥ → rūḥ (go), tgūm → gūm (get up). Where two consonants would start the word, add i-: tismaʿ → ismaʿ (listen). 'Come' and 'take' have their own forms: taʿāl, khudh.
grammar: Imperative to a man: gūm, shūf, rūḥ, taʿāl
dialogue: la, shūf is-sāʿa! iḥdaʿash w nuṣṣ
No, look at the time! Half past eleven.
OK. Listen, where did I put my phone?
Over there. Take it and come!
items: my phone: tilifōni; you'll also hear mobāyl (موبايل)
to a woman: khudhi; khudhah = take it; also said: khidh
to a woman: taʿāli; to a group: taʿālu

title: Wait a minute
goal: Ask Maryam to come and look at a problem at work, and follow her instructions.
tip: To a woman, add -i to the man's form: shūf → shūfi (look), taʿāl → taʿāli (come). In verbs like ṭarrish, the short i before the last consonant drops: ṭarrish-li → ṭarrshī-li (send me). 'Wait' (UAE) is trayya to a man, trayyi to a woman.
grammar: Imperative to a woman: add -i (taʿāli, shūfi)
dialogue: Maryam, can you help me? Come and have a look.
الإيميل ما يفتح، وما سويت شي!
il-īmēl ma yiftaḥ, w ma sawwēt shay!
The email won't open, and I didn't do anything!
Send me the email and I'll have a look.
هيه، وصل. ييب لي الملف بعد
Yes, it's come. Bring me the file too.
items: to a woman: trayyi (تريي); you'll see written اتريا; Kuwait: inṭir (انطر); never istanna (استنى)
to a woman: yībī-li (ييبي لي); you'll see written جيب لي; ييب alone also means 'he brings'
what's up? what's the matter? (also: what's wrong with it?)
about a person: shfīk? (what's wrong with you?)
can you help me? (to a man)
to a woman: tigdarīn tsāʿdīni? (تقدرين تساعديني؟)

title: Come here, everyone!
goal: Call Sēf and his friends together for a photo at Global Village: come, come closer, look, smile, let me, let's.
tip: To a group, add -u to the man's form: taʿāl → taʿālu, shūf → shūfu, garrib → garrbu (come closer; the i drops). 'Let' to a man is khallni / khallna: khallni ashūf (let me see), khallna nrūḥ (let's go); to a woman khallīni, khallīna; to a group khallūni. The next verb has no 'to'.
grammar: Imperative to a group: add -u (taʿālu, shūfu); khallni
dialogue: What's up? What do you want?
One minute, let me take your photo. Come a bit closer.
خلني أشوف. حلوة! زين سويت. يلا، خلنا نروح
khallni ashūf. ḥilwa! zēn sawwēt. yalla, khallna nrūḥ
Let me see. Lovely! Well done. Come on, let's go.
items: to one man: taʿāl; to one woman: taʿāli
to a woman: khallīni (خليني); to a group: khallūni (خلوني); khallni ashūf = let me see
aṣawwrak? = shall I take your photo? (to a man); khallūni aṣawwirkum = let me take your photo (to a group)
to one man: garrib; to one woman: garrbi
to one man: shūf; to one woman: shūfi
smile (for a photo; lit. laugh) (to a group)
to one man: iẓḥak; to one woman: iẓḥaki
to a woman: khallīna (خلينا); to a group: khallūna (خلونا); khallna nrūḥ = let's go
culture: In public places, ask before you photograph people and keep women and families you don't know out of your photos. In the UAE, taking or sharing photos of people without their consent is also against the law, with heavy fines. Many families prefer that photos of their women aren't taken or shared.

title: Don't go yet
goal: Say goodbye to Sēf at the end of the evening: don't go, don't forget, don't worry, take care.
tip: For 'don't', put la before the ordinary 'you' verb, not the command form: trūḥ → la trūḥ (don't go), tinsa → la tinsa (don't forget). To a woman the verb keeps -īn: la trūḥīn, la tḥātīn; to a group -ūn: la trūḥūn.
grammar: Don't: la + the 'you' verb (la trūḥ, la trūḥīn)
dialogue: I have to, I've got work tomorrow morning.
لا تحاتي، هذا هو. نتلاقى باكر!
la tḥāti, hādha huwa. nitlāga bāchir!
Don't worry, here it is. See you tomorrow!
مع السلامة. انتبه، لا تسوق بسرعة!
maʿa s-salāma. intibih, la tsūg b-surʿa!
Bye. Take care, don't drive fast!
items: to a woman: la trūḥīn; to a group: la trūḥūn (لا تروحون)
ʿindi dawām = I'm working (I have work); also school or university hours; ʿindi dawām bāchir: you'll see written باجر
for a feminine thing: hādhi hiya
be careful, take care (to a man)
to a woman: la tsūgīn b-surʿa
culture: Evenings in the Gulf start late, especially in summer, when the day is too hot to go out. Friends often meet after the ʿisha prayer and stay out until midnight, so ten o'clock can still be taww in-nās.

title: Checkpoint: errands with Maryam
goal: Maryam pops out to the bank: ask her to bring something back, answer her reminder and talk about what you did.
tip: This checkpoint mixes requests with the past. To a woman the command adds -i (yībī-li, khudhi), and 'don't' keeps -īn (la tḥātīn, la tinsīn). The past: ṭarrashtah (I sent it).
dialogue: سالم، عندي موعد في البنك. برجع على طول
Sālim, ʿindi mawʿid fi l-bank. barjaʿ ʿala ṭūl
Salim, I've got an appointment at the bank. I'll be straight back.
زين. ييبي لي قهوة، الله يخليج
OK. Bring me a coffee, please.
إن شاء الله. لا تنسى الإيميل والملف!
in shāʼ allāh. la tinsa l-īmēl w il-malaff!
Sure. Don't forget the email and the file!
لا تحاتين، طرشته البارحة. خذي، عشرين درهم
la tḥātīn, ṭarrashtah il-bārḥa. khudhi, ʿishrīn dirham
Don't worry, I sent it yesterday. Here, take twenty dirhams.
لا، خذي. بس لا تنسين القهوة!
la, khudhi. bas la tinsīn il-gahwa!
No, take it. But don't forget the coffee!
items: to a man: yīb-li; you'll see written جيبي لي
also 'straight on' when giving directions, and 'always, all the time'

title: Do you want to come?
goal: Invite Maryam to lunch, hear her say no, and offer to bring her something back.
tip: abi (I want) and tabi (you want) take the next verb with no 'to': abi atghadda (I want to have lunch), ma abi aṭlaʿ. To a woman, tabīn; her own verb takes -īn too: tabīn trūḥīn? (do you want to go?), but tabīn ayīb-lich shay? (do you want me to bring you something?)
grammar: Want + verb: abi atghadda, tabi trūḥ, tabīn trūḥīn
dialogue: Maryam, do you want to come with us?
The mall. I want to have lunch there.
مشكور، بس ما أبي أطلع. عندي دوام
mashkūr, bas ma abi aṭlaʿ. ʿindi dawām
Thanks, but I'd rather not go out. I'm working.
لا تحاتين. تبين أييب لج شي؟
Don't worry. Do you want me to bring you anything?
هيه، أي شي حلو. وخلها علي!
hē, ay shay ḥilu. w khallha ʿalay!
Yes, anything sweet. And it's on me!
items: do you want to go? (to a man)
to a woman: tabīn trūḥīn? (تبين تروحين؟)
where are you going? (to a group)
to one man: wēn bitrūḥ?; to one woman: wēn bitrūḥīn?
ma abi aṭlaʿ = I don't want to go out
I bring you, I'll get you (to a man)
to a woman: ayīb-lich (أييب لج); tabi ayīb-lak shay? = shall I get you something?

title: Can I help?
goal: Offer to help Maryam at the office and ask her to teach you how she makes a presentation.
tip: agdar (I can) and tigdar (you can) work like abi: the next verb follows with no 'to'. agdar asāʿdak? (can I help you? to a man), agdar asāʿdich? (to a woman). To a woman tigdar becomes tigdarīn: tigdarīn tʿallmīni? (can you teach me?)
grammar: Can + verb: agdar asāʿdak, tigdar, tigdarīn
dialogue: Sure. Can you bring me the papers?
على طول، تفضلي. شلون تقولين هذا بالعربي؟
ʿala ṭūl, tfaẓẓali. shlōn tgūlīn hādha bil-ʿarabi?
Right away, here you are. How do you say this in Arabic?
A presentation for the meeting. Do you want to learn (how)?
طبعا. يوم الأربعاء الصبح، بعد الاجتماع
ṭabʿan. yōm il-arbaʿa ṣ-ṣubḥ, baʿd il-ijtimāʿ
Of course. On Wednesday morning, after the meeting.
items: can I help you? (to a man)
to a woman: agdar asāʿdich? (أقدر أساعدج)
how do you say … in Arabic? (to a man)
to a woman: shlōn tgūlīn … bil-ʿarabi?; UAE also: chēf tgūl…; shlōn tgūl hādha bil-ʿarabi? = how do you say this in Arabic?
can you teach me? (to a man)
to a woman: tigdarīn tʿallmīni? (تقدرين تعلميني؟)
to a woman: tyībīn-li; tigdar tyīb-li…? = can you bring me…?; you'll see written تجيب لي
do you want to learn? (to a man)
also 'an offer, a deal' in shops; at work you'll also hear the English: presentation

title: What do you like?
goal: Tell Sēf what you like and don't like about life in Dubai.
tip: aḥibb (I like, I love) takes a noun or a verb with no 'to': aḥibb il-baḥar, aḥibb arūḥ il-baḥar (I like going to the beach). ʿājibni means 'I like it' (it pleases me): ish-shughul ʿājibni. Ask a man ʿājbak? and a woman ʿājbich?
grammar: Like + verb: aḥibb arūḥ, ma aḥibb; ʿājibni
dialogue: How are you? Do you like the job?
زين الحمد لله. طبعا، عاجبني وايد
zēn il-ḥamdu lillāh. ṭabʿan, ʿājibni wāyid
Fine, thank God. Of course, I like it a lot.
w shu tḥibb tsawwi baʿd id-dawām?
And what do you like doing after work?
I like going to the beach.
عادي، أروح في الليل. ما أحب البرد
ʿādi, arūḥ fi l-lēl. ma aḥibb il-bard
No big deal, I go at night. I don't like the cold.
items: do you like it?: ʿājbak? (to a man), ʿājbich? (to a woman); for a feminine thing: ʿājbatni (عاجبتني)
what do you do? / what are you doing? (to a man)
it's fine, no big deal, normal

title: Maybe, because…
goal: Answer Sēf's invitation to the desert: maybe, why, because, why not.
tip: Give a reason with ʿashān (because) and a whole sentence: ʿashān ʿindi imtiḥān (because I've got an exam). Invitations use tabi + verb: tabi tiyi? (do you want to come?). Not sure yet? yimkin (maybe), mub akīd (not sure).
grammar: Want + verb: tabi tiyi; because: ʿashān
dialogue: تبي تيي البر ويانا يوم الجمعة؟
tabi tiyi l-barr wiyyāna yōm il-jumʿa?
Do you want to come to the desert with us on Friday?
Why? What have you got on?
ʿashān ʿindi imtiḥān, w lāzim adris
Because I've got an exam, and I have to study.
No problem, we'll come back early if you want.
OK, why not! It's a deal.
items: do you want to come? (to a man)
to a woman: tabīn tiyīn? (تبين تيين؟); you'll see written تجي
also everyday: lann (لأن); fast speech: ʿshān
rāyḥīn il-barr = going out to the desert
culture: In the cooler months, roughly November to March, many Emirati families and friends drive out to il-barr at the weekend to camp, light a fire and drink gahwa. In summer it is far too hot.
